planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; Rand's goldenrod is adapted to thin, rocky, or sandy substrates and resents heavy, fertile, or poorly drained garden beds.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; this compact, clump-forming goldenrod is native to cool mountain balds, granite outcrops, and river-shore ledges of New England, the upper Midwest, and the higher Southern Appalachians, where thin soils and exposure keep competition low. It stays notably low and tidy compared to its weedier relatives, forming dense basal rosettes topped by tight clusters of golden-yellow flowers from late summer into fall, making it well suited to rock gardens, green roofs, and other sharply drained, sun-exposed sites rather than conventional perennial borders. Avoid soil amendments or supplemental fertilizer, which encourage floppy growth and invite the fungal problems this species otherwise resists in its native lean habitats.
sources: Massachusetts Natural Heritage & Endangered Species Program

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to light shade; threenerve goldenrod spreads by rhizomes once established and tolerates a wide range of soil types from sand to clay as long as drainage is adequate.

directions: Sow direct in fall or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to light shade; threenerve goldenrod is one of the most widespread goldenrods of the western United States and northern Mexico, recognizable by its upward-pointing leaves with three prominent parallel veins. Once established it is very low maintenance and drought tolerant, spreading gradually by rhizomes to form a loose colony topped by sprays of golden flowers in late summer and fall. It is a valuable late-season nectar source for bees, butterflies, and migrating monarchs in dry western gardens, and also serves as a larval host for the northern checkerspot butterfly; give it room to spread or confine it with a root barrier in smaller beds.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Elliott's goldenrod is native to coastal plain wetlands, pond margins, and wet ditches of the southeastern US and tolerates standing water better than most goldenrods.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Elliott's goldenrod is a tall, smooth-stemmed wetland species native to bogs, pond edges, marsh borders, and wet pinelands of the southeastern coastal plain from the Carolinas to Florida and west to Louisiana. Its glossy, deep green leaves and arching plumes of rich golden flowers in late summer through fall make it a strong vertical accent for rain gardens, pond margins, and other consistently damp sites where many other goldenrods struggle. It spreads modestly by rhizomes in favorable wet soil, and its abundant late-season flowers are heavily used by bees, wasps, and migrating monarch butterflies.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; pine barren goldenrod is native to dry longleaf pine sandhills and flatwoods of the southeastern coastal plain and requires sharp drainage and infertile soil to perform well.

directions: Plant in lean, dry, sharply drained sandy soil in full sun; pine barren goldenrod is native to the fire-maintained longleaf pine sandhills and flatwoods of the southeastern coastal plain, where it grows among wiregrass and other sand-adapted species. It is slender and narrow-leaved compared to many garden goldenrods, producing modest wands of golden flowers in fall that provide late-season forage for bees and other pollinators in habitats where little else is blooming. It is best suited to naturalistic sandhill or dry meadow plantings on infertile, sandy soil and should not be given rich garden soil or regular irrigation, both of which encourage disease and floppy growth.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall to allow natural cold stratification, in lean, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; this unusual goldenrod blooms in spring rather than fall and is native to coastal plain pine flatwoods of Georgia and Florida.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; spring-flowering goldenrod is a botanical curiosity among its genus, blooming in late winter and early spring rather than the late summer and fall display typical of nearly every other goldenrod species. Native to fire-maintained pine flatwoods and sandy open ground of the Florida and Georgia coastal plain, it forms a low, compact clump of narrow leaves topped by small clusters of bright yellow flowers that provide an early-season nectar source for native bees emerging before most other wildflowers have started blooming. It is best grown in naturalistic sandhill or pine-savanna style plantings on infertile, sharply drained soil, and should be kept away from rich, irrigated garden beds.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Lindheimer's beebalm is native to the limestone soils of south-central Texas and tolerates sand, gravel, and dry conditions once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or limestone-derived soil in full sun; Lindheimer's beebalm is a Texas Hill Country native named for pioneering Texas botanist Ferdinand Lindheimer, bearing erect, aromatic stems and dense, head-like clusters of pale lavender-pink tubular flowers surrounded by leafy bracts from April through June. It is notably more drought- and heat-tolerant than eastern Monarda species, making it a dependable choice for xeric and rock-garden style pollinator plantings in hot, dry climates, and it spreads modestly by rhizomes to form a loose, easily thinned colony. Bees and butterflies work the flowers heavily during its spring bloom window, and deer generally avoid the aromatic foliage.
sources: Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; basil beebalm is native to limestone glades and rocky prairies of the south-central US and self-sows readily in open, undisturbed ground.

directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, well-drained rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; basil beebalm is a small, slender annual or short-lived perennial native to limestone glades, rocky prairies, and open rocky ground across the south-central United States. Its pale lavender to whitish flowers are smaller and more delicate than those of its showier Monarda relatives, clustered in loose whorls atop wiry stems above aromatic, basil-scented foliage. It is best used in naturalistic rock garden or glade-style plantings on thin, infertile soil where it can self-sow freely from year to year, and it draws small native bees and other short-tongued pollinators during its bloom period.
sources: Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States (FSUS)

planting.note: Start indoors in late winter or direct sow in spring after frost danger passes, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Panorama Red is a reliable seed-grown strain that flowers the first year from an early start.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Panorama Red is a long-established seed-propagated bee balm strain valued for producing uniform plants with bright scarlet-red flowers reliably from seed rather than requiring division of named clones. It blooms from midsummer into early fall on sturdy, well-branched stems, and like other red-flowered Monarda didyma selections it is an outstanding hummingbird plant as well as a strong draw for bees and butterflies. Provide good air circulation and avoid letting the soil dry out for extended periods, since this cultivar shares the species' susceptibility to powdery mildew in hot, humid, or crowded conditions; dividing clumps every two to three years helps maintain vigor and airflow.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
